passage: I'm Pankaj, and this is about the fight over the cricket camp in Ooty. Last month I asked my mother, Uma, if I could go. I remember it exactly: she was at the stove, she didn't even turn round, and she said, "Forget it. You're never going to these camps." I slammed my door so hard the calendar fell. Two weeks later I brought it up again, still angry. Mummy looked shocked. "I said not this year, because of your boards. I said next summer, definitely." She remembered wiping her hands and turning to look at me. We were both completely sure. Then my sister Juhi said from the sofa, "I was there. She said 'not this year'. And you were already walking away." I still feel that "never" in my chest. But maybe my anger wrote that word in afterwards.

qa.q: What was the fight about?
qa.a: The cricket camp in Ooty.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj still feel the "never" even after hearing Juhi?
qa.a: The hurt and anger of that moment shaped the memory, so the harsher word still feels real even if it wasn't said 😔

qa.q: What turning point does Pankaj reach, and what could help in the next argument?
qa.a: Pankaj admits anger may have added the word; next time Pankaj could calmly check, "Did you mean never, or not now?", before walking away.

qa.q: How might Uma feel hearing that Pankaj remembered "never"?
qa.a: She was shocked and probably hurt, since she thought she had promised next summer and turned to look her child in the eye.

grounding: A teenager and mother each recall the same argument differently and both feel certain, with feelings reshaping the memory.

passage:
Counsellor's note, family session, Thursday
Parveen and her son Imran (16) came in about an argument from last Friday. Imran is certain she said, "If you fail maths again, don't bother coming home." Parveen is equally certain she said, "If you fail maths again, we need to talk about the phone." Both became tearful describing it. Imran remembers her shouting; Parveen remembers speaking quietly because the neighbours were over. Neither seems to be lying. Each memory looks shaped by what they felt then and what they feared afterwards.
What I did next: I asked each to begin with "I remember it this way", while the other just listened. Then I asked Parveen what she wants Imran to know now. She said, "You can always come home." Imran looked at the floor and nodded.

qa.q: What does Imran remember his mother saying?
qa.a: "If you fail maths again, don't bother coming home."

qa.q: Why might Imran remember shouting while Parveen remembers speaking quietly?
qa.a: His fear and hurt likely made her words feel loud and harsh, while she remembers her own effort to stay calm with the neighbours over.

qa.q: Which step in the session helped, and why?
qa.a: Having each begin with "I remember it this way" while the other listened; it let both memories be heard without either being called a liar.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel when Imran nods at "You can always come home"?
qa.a: She would likely feel relief and tenderness, knowing her son heard the message she most wanted him to have.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenager and his mother each certain of different words in the same argument, their memories shaped by feeling.

passage:
Dear Imran,
I owe you an apology, and a book.
When you asked about your statistics textbook last week, I was so sure. I told you I'd handed it back at the farewell party, in the corridor next to the notice board, and that you put it in your black backpack. I could see it. I even said, a bit rudely, "Check your own room first."
Yesterday I was scrolling through photos from the hostel move. There it is: me, two days after the farewell, sitting on my bed, and your textbook right there under my pillow, your name on the spine.
I was completely certain, and completely wrong. I'm sorry for making you think you'd lost it.
Coming to return it tomorrow, with samosas.
Parveen

qa.q: What did the photo from the hostel move show?
qa.a: Parveen on the bed two days after the farewell, with Imran's textbook right there under the pillow.

qa.q: How does Parveen feel after finding the photo of the textbook?
qa.a: Parveen feels sorry and embarrassed for having been so sure and for rudely telling Imran to check first, when the book was under Parveen's pillow all along.

qa.q: What could Parveen do the next time a past detail feels certain?
qa.a: Parveen could say "I think I returned it" and check photos or messages before insisting, since feeling certain isn't the same as being right.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt on being told to check the room first?
qa.a: Imran probably felt blamed and confused, starting to doubt a clear memory about a book that was never returned.

grounding: A young adult is certain of returning a book until a photo proves otherwise, showing that confidence does not measure accuracy.

passage: Nirmala, you want a story about being sure? Here's mine. I'm Gurpreet. Last winter my cousin got married in Patiala, and I was certain the wedding was on the fourteenth. Certain. I could picture the card: gold letters, fourteenth, a drawing of two elephants. I booked the night train for the thirteenth, told my professor I'd miss the fourteenth, and argued with my mother on the phone when she said, "Beta, check." "Mummy, I've seen the card." On the twelfth, my cousin sent a photo of the mehndi on her hands: "Tomorrow's the day!" I scrolled up. The card was right there in our family chat, and it said thirteenth. No elephants, just flowers. I caught the morning bus, arrived by evening, missed the pheras, and cried in the bus station. I still remember those elephants perfectly. They never existed.

qa.q: What date did the wedding card in the family chat say?
qa.a: It said thirteenth.

qa.q: Why does Gurpreet still remember the elephants perfectly?
qa.a: The memory was built so confidently that it still feels vivid, even though the card had only flowers; the sureness stayed even after the facts changed.

qa.q: What choice could have saved the trip, and why?
qa.a: Checking the card in the family chat when Mummy said "Beta, check"; looking at the record would have beaten the confident picture in Gurpreet's head.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's mother feel remembering that phone argument?
qa.a: She may feel sad that her gentle advice was brushed aside, and sorry that her child missed the pheras and cried alone.

grounding: A young adult is sure of a wedding date and a card's design until the message in the family chat proves both wrong.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 pm
Nearly had a fight with Reena at dinner. She was sure the landlord told us on the phone that the rent goes up from April. I was sure he said June. I felt my voice rising, ready to say, "You never listen properly." I stopped. Instead I said, "I remember June. But I might be wrong. Let's check." The landlord had sent a message after the call. We scrolled up. It said: "From May." Neither of us was right. We both laughed, a bit embarrassed. Reena said, "Good thing we didn't bet."
I've started typing important things into my notes right after calls. Memory is a storyteller, not a recorder. Must remember that about the bigger stuff too, like what Amma said at Christmas.
Joseph

qa.q: What did the landlord's message say?
qa.a: From May.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling just before saying "I remember June. But I might be wrong"?
qa.a: Joseph felt irritation rising and was ready to blame Reena for not listening, but chose to hold the memory lightly instead.

qa.q: Which of Joseph's choices kept the evening friendly, and why?
qa.a: Saying "I remember June, but I might be wrong. Let's check" and then reading the landlord's message; it turned a fight into a shared look at the record.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt if Joseph had said "You never listen properly"?
qa.a: She would likely have felt insulted and defensive, and the argument might have grown, even though they were both wrong.

grounding: A young adult says 'I remember it this way', checks a written record, and lets a sibling's different memory stand without blame.

passage: In their flat in Kyoto, Noa's cousin Ren loved one joke. "Noa, remember when the monkey stole your hat at the zoo?" Noa, five, had never been to the zoo. "No!" she said. A week later: "Remember the monkey? It ran up the tree!" Noa thought. "Maybe." By the third visit, Noa told her father, Hiroshi, "A monkey took my yellow hat and ran up a tree, and I cried." Hiroshi put down his chopsticks. "Noa, we've never been to the zoo." Noa looked confused. "But I remember the tree." Hiroshi gently asked Ren to stop the joke. That weekend he took Noa to the real zoo, and she held her yellow hat tightly.

qa.q: Where had Noa never been?
qa.a: To the zoo.

qa.q: Why does Noa say "But I remember the tree"?
qa.a: Being asked again and again made her imagine the scene, and the imagined picture now feels like a real memory to her.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi do after realising what had happened, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He gently asked Ren to stop the joke so the story wouldn't keep growing, and he didn't scold Noa, since she wasn't lying.

qa.q: How might Ren feel when asked to stop the joke?
qa.a: Ren might feel surprised and a little guilty, not having realised a joke could become something Noa truly believed.

grounding: A preschool girl repeatedly asked about a zoo trip that never happened begins to describe it as a real memory.

passage: At the kindergarten, Hafsa, the new assistant, had wrongly heard that Nitin had a birthday party at the weekend. On Monday she asked, "Nitin, did you have a big cake at your party?" Nitin, four, shook his head. On Tuesday: "Was it a train cake, with candles?" "Maybe." By Thursday, at circle time, Nitin announced, "My train cake had blue smoke, and I blew out five candles!" At pickup his mother looked puzzled. "His birthday's in March. There was no party." Hafsa's face fell. From then on she asked children only, "What did you do at the weekend?"

qa.q: When is Nitin's birthday?
qa.a: His birthday's in March.

qa.q: How did Nitin seem to feel when describing the train cake, and why?
qa.a: Nitin seemed excited and proud announcing the blue smoke and five candles, because Hafsa's repeated questions had made the imagined party feel like a memory.

qa.q: What change did Hafsa make, and why does it help?
qa.a: She began asking only open questions like "What did you do at the weekend?", which don't put ideas into a young child's head.

qa.q: How might Nitin's mother feel hearing about the party that never happened?
qa.a: She was puzzled and perhaps a little worried at first, then likely relieved to understand where the story came from.

grounding: A preschooler repeatedly asked about a party that never happened starts describing it in vivid detail.

passage: At the village school near Sehore, someone had left the garden gate open, and the headmaster's goat had eaten all the marigolds. Avni and Kashish cornered Keshav by the handpump. "You were near the gate, na? You saw Raju open it, didn't you? He had his red cap on, na?" Keshav, nine, had been feeding tiffin crumbs to the sparrows. He hadn't seen anything. But the girls kept asking, closer and closer, and a picture came: a red cap, a hand on the latch. By afternoon he told the headmaster, "Raju opened it. He had his red cap." Raju burst into tears; he'd been absent that morning. The headmaster sat Keshav down on the verandah. "Tell me only what you saw yourself, from the start." Keshav was quiet a long time. "Sparrows," he said. "I saw sparrows."

qa.q: What had the headmaster's goat eaten?
qa.a: All the marigolds.

qa.q: Why did Keshav come to believe he saw Raju's red cap?
qa.a: Keshav felt pressured as Avni and Kashish kept asking leading questions about the cap and the latch, until the picture they described slowly became his own.

qa.q: What did the headmaster do that brought out the truth?
qa.a: He asked Keshav to tell only what he had seen himself, from the start, an open question that didn't suggest any answer.

qa.q: What was it like for Raju to be blamed?
qa.a: Raju was hurt and frightened, accused of something he couldn't have done since he was absent that morning.

grounding: A boy pressed with leading questions by classmates takes on a detail he never saw, until an open question brings back his own memory.

passage: After Saturday practice in Soweto, the clubhouse window was found cracked. Coach Zanele crouched in front of Omar, ten, who had been packing the cones. "You saw the older boys from the other club kicking balls at it, didn't you? Hard kicks, near the window?" Omar hesitated. He had seen balls, somewhere. "I think so." "The tall one in the green bib?" "...Yes. The green bib." By Monday Omar was telling his mother the whole scene: the tall boy, the crack, the laughing. His mother listened, then asked, "What did you see with your own eyes, before Coach asked you?" Omar opened his mouth and closed it. "I was packing cones. I heard a bang. That's all." He looked at the floor. "But the green bib feels real, Ma."

qa.q: What was Omar doing after practice?
qa.a: Packing the cones.

qa.q: How does Omar feel when his mother asks what he saw himself, and what shows it?
qa.a: Omar feels confused and uncomfortable, looking at the floor after admitting he only heard a bang, yet saying the green bib still feels real.

qa.q: Which question from Omar's mother helped, and why?
qa.a: "What did you see with your own eyes, before Coach asked you?" It was open and neutral, helping Omar separate what he saw from what was suggested.

qa.q: How might the tall boy in the green bib be affected if Omar's first story were believed?
qa.a: He could be blamed and punished for a window he may never have touched, all because of a suggested detail.

grounding: A boy questioned with leading words by his coach adopts details he never saw, until his mother asks an open question.

passage: I'm Tanuja, Nikita's older sister. Nikita's class went to Bhimtal lake last month. Nikita was in the second boat with her friend Pooja; the drama happened in the first boat. I know because Nikita phoned me that night: "Didi, did you hear? A snake swam next to Juhi's boat and Mohan almost fell in!" Since then her friends have told the story at our house twice, louder each time, the snake getting longer. Yesterday Nikita told our cousins, "The snake swam right past me, and I grabbed Mohan's shirt so he wouldn't fall." She said it with total certainty, eyes wide. I reminded her she was in the second boat. She frowned. "No, I was there. I can see its head in the water." I don't think she's lying. I think she's heard it so often it's become hers.

qa.q: Which boat was Nikita in?
qa.a: The second boat, with her friend Pooja.

qa.q: How does Nikita feel about being in the snake story, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nikita feels completely sure and excited, telling it with wide eyes and frowning when reminded she was in the second boat, because her friends' retellings blended into her memory.

qa.q: How could Tanuja help Nikita without calling her a liar?
qa.a: Tanuja could explain that group stories often blend into our own memories, and suggest asking Pooja what the second boat actually saw.

qa.q: How might Mohan feel hearing Nikita say she grabbed his shirt?
qa.a: Mohan might be confused, since he remembers no one from the other boat grabbing him, and may wonder where the detail came from.

grounding: A sister watches a teenager come to remember a boat incident she only heard friends describe, as group retelling blends into her memory.

passage:
Wednesday: The fire alarm rang during chemistry lab. Rukmini, fifteen, was in the washroom down the corridor and came out to find everyone lined up on the field. Aparna whispered, "A test tube cracked on the burner. Smoke everywhere."
Thursday: At lunch the story grew. "It was a small explosion," someone said. "Glass flew," said another. "Sir's eyebrows got singed!" Everyone laughed. Rukmini laughed too, picturing it.
Monday: At dinner Rukmini told her mother, "I was right there when the test tube blew up. A bit of glass hit my sleeve." Her mother looked alarmed. Aparna, visiting, put down her spoon. "Rukku, you were in the washroom." Rukmini opened her mouth to argue, then stopped. She could see the glass. She just couldn't remember seeing it.

qa.q: Where was Rukmini when the fire alarm rang?
qa.a: In the washroom down the corridor.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini feel sure, at dinner, that she had seen the glass?
qa.a: She pictured it while laughing with her friends, and that imagined picture blended into her memory until it felt like her own.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do when Aparna corrected her, and why was that a good choice?

qa.q: What is it like for Aparna to hear Rukmini retell a scene she missed?
qa.a: Aparna is startled enough to put down her spoon; she knows where Rukmini really was, so she has to speak up gently and correct a friend in front of her mother.

grounding: Over several days, a teenager who missed a lab incident absorbs her friends' retellings and comes to remember being there.

It walked right into this courtyard, spread its tail, and I fed it a bit of my roti. I can still hear it screaming." Nani laughed. "No peacock ever came here, beti. Never." Irawati's mother shook her head too.
Monday: Back at college, Irawati couldn't let it go. She told her friend Asif, "I can see the blue of its neck. How can that not be real?" Asif shrugged. "Maybe you saw one somewhere else?"
Thursday: Her mother phoned. She had found an old album: Irawati, four, at a zoo in Delhi, holding roti out to a peacock behind a fence. Irawati looked at the photo for a long time. The feeling was real. The courtyard wasn't.

qa.q: What did Irawati say she fed the peacock?
qa.a: A bit of her roti.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Nani said no peacock came, and why?
qa.a: Irawati felt puzzled and unsettled, unable to let it go, because she could still see the blue of its neck and hear it scream.

qa.q: What did the old photo show, and how could Irawati use that lesson?
qa.a: It showed her feeding a peacock at a zoo in Delhi; she could remember that vivid details can be real pieces placed in the wrong scene, and check before insisting.

qa.q: What might Nani have felt when Irawati insisted about the courtyard?
qa.a: Nani was probably amused but certain, knowing her own courtyard well, and perhaps curious where the story came from 🙂

grounding: A young woman vividly recalls a childhood scene her family says never happened there, learning that vividness does not prove accuracy.

passage: Simran, beti, you told that well story again at dinner, eyes shining: you, six years old, falling into the farm well, the cold water, your Dadu pulling you out by your plait. You told it so well your cousins went quiet. Now let your Rekha Dadi tell you what I remember, since I was there. There was no fall. It was your cousin Gunjan who slipped into the irrigation channel, knee-deep, and your Dadu lifted her out, laughing. You were on the charpai with me, eating a guava, and you cried because everyone ran to Gunjan. For years afterwards you begged to hear that story. Somewhere along the way it became yours. I'm not saying you're lying, beti. Your heart remembers the fright. But a memory can be bright and strong and still not have happened.

qa.q: Who actually slipped into the irrigation channel?
qa.a: Her cousin Gunjan, knee-deep.

qa.q: Why does Simran's well story feel so real to her?
qa.a: She heard the family story so often and felt the fright of that day so strongly that the vivid version became her own memory.

qa.q: How could Simran hold this memory differently from now on?
qa.a: She could treat the feeling as real but the details as uncertain, and check with family before telling it as fact.

qa.q: What might it be like for Gunjan to hear Simran tell the story as her own?
qa.a: Gunjan might be puzzled or a little put out, hearing her own scary moment told as someone else's.

grounding: A grandmother tells a young woman that her vivid, emotional childhood memory of falling into a well never happened to her.

passage:
Headmistress's note, Tuesday
At lunch, Yusuf (Class 2) came to Ms Reena crying, with a scraped knee, and said, "Someone pushed me on the stairs." Two children crowding round said, "It was Kunal, wasn't it?" Ms Reena didn't repeat the name. She knelt, cleaned the knee from the first-aid box and said, "I can see you're really upset. Tell me what happened, from the start." Yusuf said he was running down, someone's bag bumped him, and he fell. He didn't know whose. Ms Reena wrote his exact words and the time on a slip before the bell, spoke to the children on the stairs one at a time with the same open question, and phoned Yusuf's mother that afternoon. It turned out to be an accidental bump from a Class 5 bag. Yusuf's hurt was real; Kunal hadn't been there at all.

qa.q: What did Ms Reena write on the slip?
qa.a: Yusuf's exact words and the time.

qa.q: How did Ms Reena respond to Yusuf's feelings, and why didn't she repeat Kunal's name?
qa.a: Ms Reena named that Yusuf was really upset and stayed calm and careful, not repeating Kunal's name so as not to plant the idea in his account.

qa.q: Which of Ms Reena's steps protected the truth, and why?
qa.a: Asking each child the same open question one at a time and writing down Yusuf's words straight away, before the story could shift.

qa.q: What would have happened to Kunal if Ms Reena had asked "It was Kunal who pushed you, wasn't it?"
qa.a: Yusuf might have agreed, and Kunal could have been blamed and punished for something Kunal had no part in.

grounding: A young teacher avoids leading questions, writes down a child's words at once, and treats his hurt as real without taking every detail as proof.

passage:
Sunday night
Long call with Indu. She's been carrying something about Papa for years: that when she failed Class 11 chemistry, he said, "You'll never amount to anything." She was crying on the phone. My first reaction was, "Papa would never say that." I didn't say it. I remember that evening differently: I remember him saying, "This isn't like you." But I was twelve and in the next room.
What I did say: "That sounds like it really hurt. I'm sorry." And I asked, "What would help now?", not "Are you sure he said that?" She wants to talk to Papa herself. I said I'd sit with her if she wanted.
Writing this down tonight, while it's fresh, so I don't turn it into my own version later.
Vaibhav

qa.q: What does Indu remember Papa saying when she failed Class 11 chemistry?
qa.a: "You'll never amount to anything."

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel during the call with Indu, and what was held back?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt doubtful, thinking Papa would never say that, but also caring, so Vaibhav held the doubt back and told Indu it sounded like it really hurt.

qa.q: Which of Vaibhav's choices on the call helped Indu most, and why?
qa.a: Saying "That sounds like it really hurt" and asking what would help, treating her feeling as real without demanding proof of the exact words.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt if Vaibhav had asked "Are you sure he said that?"
qa.a: She would likely have felt disbelieved and more alone, as if her hurt didn't count unless every word was proven 🤍

grounding: A young adult treats a sibling's painful family memory as real without arguing details, avoids leading questions and writes things down while fresh.

passage: At the city library's children's corner, Gargi, the librarian, asked what everyone did at the weekend. Chirag, five, shot up his hand. "I saw a monster in the park! Gargi didn't laugh. "Chirag, where did you meet it: in the park, or in a book?" "In the park." Then his eyes found the purple cover on the shelf. "Ohh. That one." He grinned. "It was in the park in the book."

qa.a: It ate the swings.

qa.q: Why was Chirag so sure he met the monster in the park?
qa.a: He remembered the monster and the park clearly but had lost track that both came from the picture book, so it felt like something he saw.

qa.q: How did Gargi help Chirag find where the monster came from?
qa.a: Gargi didn't laugh and asked a gentle either-or question, park or book, which gave him space to notice the cover and sort it out himself.

qa.q: Why did Neelam catch Gargi's eye when Chirag spoke?
qa.a: Neelam recognised the monster from the book she read on Friday and wanted Gargi to know the story's real source.

qa.a: In the old tamarind tree.

qa.q: Why did Ojas tell the class about the monster so confidently?

passage: In their village near Karad, Hrithik, eight, came home bursting with news for his older brother Tejas. "At school today, the headmaster's bicycle rolled down the slope, flew over the fence and landed in the pond with a big splash! Frogs jumped out!" Tejas laughed. "That's from the cartoon we watched last night, the one with the mouse on the bicycle." "No! It happened at school. I saw it." Hrithik's face went red and his eyes filled up. "Why don't you believe me?" Next morning Tejas asked the headmaster's son, Vikram, who said the bicycle had been parked by the office all day. Hrithik listened, confused. "But I remember the splash," he whispered. He wasn't lying. He just couldn't find where the splash had come from.

qa.q: Where had the headmaster's bicycle been all day, according to Vikram?
qa.a: Parked by the office all day.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik's eyes fill up when Tejas laughed?
qa.a: He sincerely believed it happened at school, so being doubted felt unfair and hurtful 😢

qa.q: How could Tejas help Hrithik next time without making him feel called a liar?
qa.a: Tejas could gently ask where Hrithik first saw it, at school or in the cartoon, and say that everyone mixes up where things came from sometimes.

qa.q: What might Vikram have thought about the flying-bicycle story?
qa.a: Vikram probably found it funny and strange, knowing his father's bicycle never moved from the office.

grounding: A boy sincerely insists a cartoon scene happened at school, having lost track of where the memory came from.

passage: In a primary school in Valencia, Mateo, nine, told his classmate Layla at break, "Remember when Pip the hamster escaped last week and drove the toy car all the way down the corridor? Everyone screamed!" Layla stared. "That never happened. Pip was in the cage the whole time." "It did! I saw it!" Mateo turned to their teacher, Sofia. "Miss, tell her!" Sofia thought for a moment. "Mateo, I think I know that hamster. Wasn't it in the cartoon we watched on Friday, the one about the pet shop?" Mateo opened his mouth, then closed it. The toy car, the corridor, the screaming: all of it was the cartoon. "But it felt like our school," he said slowly. "It felt like Pip."

qa.q: Where was Pip the whole time, according to Layla?
qa.a: Pip was in the cage the whole time.

qa.q: Why did Mateo ask Sofia to back him up?
qa.a: He sincerely believed it happened at school and felt frustrated that Layla didn't believe him.

qa.q: How did Sofia help Mateo find the real source, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gently suggested the cartoon they watched on Friday instead of calling him a liar, which let him check the memory himself.

qa.q: How might Layla feel when Mateo realises it was the cartoon?
qa.a: Layla might feel relieved to be right but also understanding, seeing that Mateo truly believed it.

grounding: A boy sincerely defends a cartoon scene as something that happened at school, because the source of the memory has been lost.
